tool_args.old_string: SmolVLA's pixel-shuffle $4{\times}4$ folding concatenates 16 patches per token (Figure~\ref{fig:pixel_shuffle}), creating non-overlapping receptive fields. tool_args.new_string: SmolVLA's pixel-shuffle $4{\times}4$ folding concatenates 16 patches per token (Figure~\ref{fig:pixel_shuffle}), creating non-overlapping receptive fields. Removing any token eliminates an entire spatial block, collapsing SR to ${\leq}$6.6\% at $k{=}0.95$ across all suites and methods (verified on two checkpoints; Appendix~\ref{app:smolvla_ablation}). Notably, X-VLA's BART encoder is also entangling, yet far more robust: its 12-layer self-attention redistributes information across tokens, creating inter-token redundancy that buffers against removal. Pixel-shuffle, by contrast, performs a fixed deterministic fold with no learned information sharing---each output token's receptive field is disjoint, leaving zero redundancy for pruning to exploit. This contrast shows that entanglement per se does not predict fragility; the relevant factor is whether the connector creates redundancy across its output tokens.

tool_args.old_string: $\pi_{0.5}$'s random pruning at $k{=}0.9$ collapses to 9.0\% on Object despite removing only 10\% of tokens. We compare hard pruning (removes tokens, re-indexes positions) with zero-masking (zeros embeddings, preserves positions): zero-masking preserves 98.0\% SR while hard pruning collapses to 9.0\%. On $\pi_{0.5}$, the 89\,pp gap is entirely attributable to position disruption: its linear connector tolerates complete signal destruction but not index shifts. This ablation targets $\pi_{0.5}$ because its RoPE-based position encoding is most susceptible to re-indexing; other connectors use different positional mechanisms.
tool_args.new_string:
$\pi_{0.5}$'s random pruning at $k{=}0.9$ collapses to 9.0\% on Object despite removing only 10\% of tokens. We compare hard pruning (removes tokens, re-indexes positions) with zero-masking (zeros embeddings, preserves positions): zero-masking preserves 98.0\% SR while hard pruning collapses to 9.0\%. On $\pi_{0.5}$, the 89\,pp gap is entirely attributable to position disruption: its linear connector tolerates complete signal destruction but not index shifts. This ablation targets $\pi_{0.5}$ because its RoPE-based position encoding is most susceptible to re-indexing; other connectors use different positional mechanisms.

This finding has practical implications: for position-sensitive architectures, any compression scheme that alters the token sequence length---including token merging---will disrupt positional encodings. Compression strategies for such models must either preserve the original sequence length (e.g., zero-masking or learned re-encoding) or include position-aware mechanisms that compensate for index shifts.

tool_args.new_string:
VTR uses $M$ learned queries cross-attending over all 128 source tokens (${\sim}$22M parameters, $<$5\% of SmolVLA). At 75\% compression, VTR achieves 60.1 $\pm$ 1.3\% SR ($M{=}32$, $n{=}3$; Table~\ref{tab:vtr_main}), exceeding the unpruned LoRA baseline (44.8\%) by 15.3\,pp. An extended training control rules out additional optimization as the source ($p > 0.9$; Appendix~\ref{app:smart_compress_details}). A parameter-matched MLP adapter achieves 63.4 $\pm$ 2.6\% ($p{=}0.15$), indicating the benefit stems from re-encoding rather than the specific cross-attention mechanism. This suggests the key ingredient is providing a learnable interface between the entangled connector output and the LLM input, allowing the model to reconstruct a compressed representation that respects the LLM's positional expectations.

Performance scales gracefully with compression: reducing $M$ from 32 to 16 (87.5\% compression) costs only 3.2\,pp, while still exceeding the unpruned baseline by 12.1\,pp. Cross-suite generalization confirms the learned compression transfers: Spatial recovers to 53.2\% and Goal to 56.4\%, both from 0.0\% under hard pruning, without suite-specific training. For $\pi_{0.5}$, the compression opportunity takes a different form: $k{=}0.9$ with L2 scoring cuts attention FLOPs by ${\sim}$16\% while preserving full SR, requiring no additional parameters or training.

tool_args.old_string: We set out to understand why identical token pruning produces dramatically different outcomes across VLA architectures. The vision-language connector emerges as the strongest predictor: its coefficient of variation (CV), computable from a single forward pass, partitions architectures into compressibility regimes. Token-independent connectors degrade gracefully while entangling connectors exhibit catastrophic cliffs amplified by task complexity (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}). No scoring method is universally safe---the importance margin follows an inverted-U curve that reverses at aggressive ratios---and position disruption, not information loss, is the binding constraint. For connectors where all deletion fails, VTR recovers baseline performance at 75\% compression. Practitioners should evaluate CV before deploying any pruning strategy; real-robot validation and adaptive per-task compression remain open.
tool_args.new_string:
We set out to understand why identical token pruning produces dramatically different outcomes across VLA architectures. The vision-language connector emerges as the strongest predictor: its coefficient of variation (CV), computable from a single forward pass, partitions architectures into compressibility regimes. Token-independent connectors degrade gracefully while entangling connectors exhibit catastrophic cliffs amplified by task complexity (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}). No scoring method is universally safe---the importance margin follows an inverted-U curve that reverses at aggressive ratios---and position disruption, not information loss, is the binding constraint. For connectors where all deletion fails, VTR recovers baseline performance at 75\% compression.

These findings suggest a practical decision procedure for VLA deployment. First, compute CV from a single forward pass to identify the compressibility regime. For low-CV architectures (CV$\,{<}\,$0.15), L2 scoring at conservative ratios ($k{\geq}0.85$) delivers safe compression with no retraining, but practitioners must verify that position re-indexing does not cause catastrophic failure. For high-CV architectures (CV$\,{>}\,$0.20), hard pruning is unreliable regardless of scoring method; learned re-encoding (VTR or similar) is required. Between these regimes, task-specific validation is essential, as scoring method effectiveness varies with both connector type and task complexity. Real-robot validation and adaptive per-task compression remain important open directions.

tool_args.old_string: All evaluations use LIBERO simulation; real-robot validation would strengthen applicability. The six architectures differ in backbone and scale beyond the connector, preventing full causal isolation. CV relies on four closed-loop models; expanding the pool will test universality. VTR is validated on SmolVLA only. Most conditions use a single seed ($\pi_{0.5}$ Long: $n{=}5$, s.d.\ ${\leq}$2.7\,pp).
tool_args.new_string: All evaluations use LIBERO simulation; real-robot transfer introduces additional factors (sensor noise, latency, contact dynamics) that may interact with compression. The six architectures differ in backbone size (450M--7B), action head design, and training data beyond the connector, preventing full causal isolation of the connector effect. CV as a diagnostic relies on four closed-loop models spanning three connector families; while the monotonic relationship is consistent, expanding to additional architectures (e.g., diffusion-based VLAs, architectures with dynamic token counts) will test universality. VTR is validated on SmolVLA only; whether learned re-encoding generalizes to other entangling connectors (e.g., Q-Former-style cross-attention) remains open. Most conditions use a single evaluation seed; while the five-seed condition on $\pi_{0.5}$ Long shows low variance (s.d.\ ${\leq}$2.7\,pp), single-seed results on other models may understate variability, particularly near cliff transitions.

══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
检查范围
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
每个东西第一次出现的位置，必须已经完成定义。包括：
□ 缩写 / 简写（如 RLHF / DPO / IRT，第一次出现要写全称 + 缩写）
□ 自定义概念 / 术语（你 paper 自己造的词，如 "behavioral death"、"sycophancy score"）
□ 数学符号 / 公式中的变量（每个变量在第一次出现的方程里就要解释）
□ 自定义方法 / 模块组件（"the consistency gate"、"the alignment head"）
□ 评测指标（自定义的 metric，必须在 main result 表出现之前定义清楚）
□ 数据集 / setting 的内部命名（"the strict split"、"the holdout pool"）
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
常见违规模式
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
❌ Abstract / Intro 里用了一个自造术语，Method 才定义
❌ Intro 提到 "we use SYCONScore"，到 §4 才看到这个 metric 的定义
❌ Method §2 用了变量 α，到 §2.3 才写 "where α denotes..."
❌ Method 提到 "module M"，结构图 + 解释在 Appendix 才有
❌ Table 1 列了 "Score@K"，K 在 §5 才说取什么值
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
修复策略
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
每个违规位置二选一：
A) 把定义提前到第一次使用之前。最干净。
B) 在第一次使用的位置加一个简短的 inline 解释（一句话 / 括号说明）+ "(formally defined in §X)" 引用前向。容忍度更高的妥协方案。
注意：A 优先。只有 A 会改动太多结构时，才退而求其次用 B。

tool_args.old_string:
We set out to understand why identical token pruning produces dramatically different outcomes across VLA architectures. The vision-language connector emerges as the strongest predictor: its coefficient of variation (CV), computable from a single forward pass, partitions architectures into compressibility regimes. Token-independent connectors degrade gracefully while entangling connectors exhibit catastrophic cliffs amplified by task complexity (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}). No scoring method is universally safe---the importance margin follows an inverted-U curve that reverses at aggressive ratios---and position disruption, not information loss, is the binding constraint. For connectors where all deletion fails, VTR recovers baseline performance at 75\% compression.

These findings suggest a practical decision procedure for VLA deployment. First, compute CV from a single forward pass to identify the compressibility regime. For low-CV architectures (CV$\,{<}\,$0.15), L2 scoring at conservative ratios ($k{\geq}0.85$) delivers safe compression with no retraining, but practitioners must verify that position re-indexing does not cause catastrophic failure. For high-CV architectures (CV$\,{>}\,$0.20), hard pruning is unreliable regardless of scoring method; learned re-encoding (VTR or similar) is required. Between these regimes, scoring method effectiveness varies with both connector type and task complexity.
tool_args.new_string: We set out to understand why identical token pruning produces dramatically different outcomes across VLA architectures. The vision-language connector emerges as the strongest predictor: its coefficient of variation (CV), computable from a single forward pass, partitions architectures into compressibility regimes. Token-independent connectors degrade gracefully while entangling connectors exhibit catastrophic cliffs amplified by task complexity (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}). No scoring method is universally safe---the importance margin follows an inverted-U curve that reverses at aggressive ratios---and position disruption, not information loss, is the binding constraint. For connectors where all deletion fails, VTR recovers baseline performance at 75\% compression. Practitioners should compute CV before deploying any pruning strategy to identify the appropriate compression regime for their architecture.

tool_args.old_string: All evaluations use LIBERO simulation; real-robot transfer introduces sensor noise, latency, and contact dynamics that may interact with compression. The six architectures differ in backbone size (450M--7B) and training data beyond the connector, preventing full causal isolation. CV as a diagnostic relies on four closed-loop models; expanding to additional architectures (e.g., diffusion-based VLAs) will test universality. VTR is validated on SmolVLA only. Most conditions use a single seed ($\pi_{0.5}$ Long: $n{=}5$, s.d.\ ${\leq}$2.7\,pp); single-seed results near cliff transitions may understate variability.
tool_args.new_string: All evaluations use LIBERO simulation; real-robot validation with sensor noise and contact dynamics would further strengthen applicability. Most conditions use a single evaluation seed ($\pi_{0.5}$ Long: $n{=}5$, s.d.\ ${\leq}$2.7\,pp); additional seeds on other models would tighten confidence intervals. VTR is validated on SmolVLA; extending to other entangling connectors is a natural next step.
